data.body:
## My monitor was testing the wrong commit -- corrected, and the reasoning is worth keeping

A FAILED(ACTIONABLE, non-scanner) event fired on run 33845037133 with
test_emitted_bpmn_has_no_illegal_ids crashing a worker -- on a run whose headSha (6b034b9f8224)
CONTAINS the 9a17 fix. That reads as a genuine recurrence.

It is not. The run is change 2606 patchset 4, and that patchset's PARENT is 6125c5345f01, which
PREDATES 668523feffde. So its test code is the old in-fixture provisioning and the crash is expected.

THE FLAW WAS MINE: for a Gerrit patchset run, headSha is MAIN'S TIP -- the trusted-main workflow
source -- not the patchset's base. My ancestor test was therefore asking 'does main have the fix?'
(now always yes) rather than 'does this patchset's code have the fix?'. It would have false-alarmed on
every old-base change indefinitely AND, more seriously, could never have distinguished a real
recurrence from an expected one. A filter that cannot produce a negative is not a filter.

The galling part: I identified the workflow-vs-test-code distinction hours earlier, wrote it into the
loop prompt, explained it to two agents -- and then built a filter that ignored it. Knowing a fact
and encoding it in the tool that depends on it are different acts.

FIXED: the monitor now extracts refs/changes/N/C/P from the run log, fetches that patchset from
gerrit, and tests ITS base against the fix. Branch-head runs still report unconditionally, since
there headSha genuinely IS the code under test. Scanner-only failures stay suppressed.

Third and final tuning of this watch. Each round removed a class of false signal: pre-fix noise, then
the owned scanner blocker, now old-base patchsets. Stopping here -- further tuning would be polishing
rather than protecting, and the remaining reports are ones I would want woken for.
